## Purpose

This procedure describes the field measurement of soil infiltration
rate using single-ring and double-ring infiltrometers. Infiltration
rate is the velocity at which water enters the soil surface, typically
expressed in cm/h or mm/h. It is a key parameter for evaluating
stormwater management, irrigation efficiency, soil compaction,
hydrologic modeling, and land use impacts on soil physical properties.
The double-ring method follows ASTM D3385 [@astm_d3385_2018]; the
single-ring method follows @bouwer1986. Infiltration measurements are
also essential for calibrating hydrologic models and for evaluating
the effects of soil sealing in urban environments [@hillel1998;
@reynolds2002].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Field measurement of infiltration rate on mineral
  soils at all EA Program sites, including agricultural plots,
  photovoltaic panel study sites, restoration areas, and urban soils
- **Does not apply to:** Soils with very low hydraulic conductivity
  (less than 1 x 10^-5^ cm/s; see ASTM D5093 for sealed-inner-ring
  method); rocky or gravelly soils that prevent ring insertion;
  laboratory column permeability tests
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve sampling plan, ensure training compliance |
| Field Lead        | Coordinate logistics, select test locations  |
| Trained Personnel | Conduct infiltration tests per this SOP      |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent testing |

## Definitions

- **Double-ring infiltrometer:** A measurement apparatus consisting of
  two concentric steel rings driven into the soil surface; the inner
  ring provides the measurement zone; the outer ring creates a buffer
  that minimizes lateral flow from the inner ring, enforcing
  predominantly vertical infiltration.
- **Final infiltration rate (steady-state rate):** The constant rate at
  which water enters the soil after the soil profile is saturated and
  the infiltration rate has stabilized; approximates the saturated
  hydraulic conductivity ($K_{sat}$) of the surface soil.
- **Green-Ampt model:** A physically based infiltration model that
  describes the rate of water entry into soil as a function of
  saturated hydraulic conductivity, matric suction at the wetting
  front, and soil moisture deficit; used to interpret falling-head
  infiltration data.
- **Infiltration rate:** The volumetric flux of water entering the soil
  surface per unit area per unit time, expressed in mm h^-1^ or
  cm h^-1^; decreases from an initially high rate in dry soil to a
  lower, stable final rate as the soil wets.
- **Macropore flow:** Preferential movement of water through large
  continuous pores (earthworm burrows, root channels, structural
  cracks); produces non-uniform wetting and anomalously high initial
  infiltration rates that do not reflect bulk soil hydraulic
  conductivity.
- **Matric potential:** The energy status of soil water due to capillary
  and adsorptive forces; expressed in kPa or cm H~2~O; drives water
  movement from wet to dry zones during infiltration.
- **Saturated hydraulic conductivity ($K_{sat}$):** The proportionality
  constant in Darcy's law relating water flux to hydraulic gradient
  under saturated conditions; the primary soil hydraulic property
  controlling drainage, runoff, and deep percolation; approximated by
  the steady-state infiltration rate.
- **Single-ring infiltrometer:** A simplified apparatus using one ring
  driven into the soil; easier to deploy than double-ring but subject
  to lateral flow error; appropriate for screening or comparative
  measurements when absolute $K_{sat}$ is not required.
  

## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Driving metal rings into the soil with a sledge or mallet
  poses a risk of hand, finger, and foot injury. The rings have sharp
  edges.
- **Ergonomic:** Carrying water containers (20 L jugs) and rings to
  remote field sites can cause strain.
- **Environmental:** Standard field hazards (heat exposure, uneven
  terrain, insects).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots (steel-toed preferred when
  driving rings)
- [ ] Leather work gloves (when handling rings and sledge)
- [ ] Safety glasses (when driving rings)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Related SOPs

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) for general
field safety procedures.


## Equipment and Materials

### Method A: Double-Ring Infiltrometer (ASTM D3385)

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Inner ring                    | Minimum 30 cm (12 in) diameter, 20 cm tall; 14-gauge or heavier steel |
| Outer ring                    | Minimum 60 cm (24 in) diameter, 20 cm tall; same gauge as inner ring |
| Sledge hammer (3--5 kg)       | For driving rings                         |
| Driving cap or wooden plank   | Placed on top of the ring to distribute hammer blows evenly and prevent ring deformation |
| Carpenter's level             | For checking ring verticality             |
| Ruler or graduated staff (mm) | For measuring water level in the inner ring |
| Stopwatch or timer            | For recording time intervals              |
| Water supply                  | 40--80 L per test; carry in jerrycans or connect to a portable tank |
| Bucket or pitcher             | For filling rings without disturbing the soil surface |
| Plastic sheeting or burlap    | Placed inside the ring during initial filling to prevent soil disturbance |
| Mariotte bottle (optional)    | For maintaining constant head automatically |
| Field data sheet              | Printed from Appendix A                   |
| Clipboard and pencil          | Mechanical pencil preferred               |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording test locations               |
| Tape measure                  | For measuring ring insertion depth         |

### Method B: Single-Ring Infiltrometer

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Single ring                   | 30 cm diameter minimum (larger is better; 90 cm preferred for accuracy); 20 cm tall |
| All other equipment           | Same as Method A, minus the outer ring    |


## Procedure

### Site Selection and Preparation

1. Select test locations based on the project sampling plan. Avoid
   locations with visible animal burrows, large root channels, cracks,
   or other macropore features unless the objective is specifically to
   characterize preferential flow.
2. Record GPS coordinates and site description
3. Clear surface litter and loose organic debris from a 1 x 1 m area
   without disturbing the mineral soil surface
4. Note antecedent conditions in the field notebook: recent rainfall,
   soil moisture (qualitative: dry, moist, wet), and surface condition
   (bare, vegetated, crusted)

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
Collect a companion bulk density core
([SOP-F402](SOP-F402-soil-bulk-density.qmd)) and a texture-by-feel
assessment ([SOP-F401](SOP-F401-soil-texture-by-feel.qmd)) at each
infiltration test location. These measurements help interpret the
infiltration results.
:::

### Ring Installation -- Double-Ring Method

1. Center the inner ring at the test location
2. Place the driving cap or wooden plank on top of the ring
3. Drive the inner ring vertically into the soil to a depth of
   approximately 5--10 cm (2--4 in) using even blows from the sledge.
   Avoid tilting the ring; check periodically with the level.
4. Measure and record the insertion depth on at least two sides
5. Center the outer ring around the inner ring. Drive it to
   approximately 10--15 cm (4--6 in), deeper than the inner ring, to
   prevent test water from escaping beneath the outer ring.
6. Check that the inner ring is still centered and level

::: {.callout-important}
Do not drive the rings deeper than necessary. Over-driving compresses
the soil along the ring walls and creates an artificial seal that
reduces measured infiltration rates. If the soil cracks or separates
from the ring wall, abandon the test location and start at a new spot.
:::

### Ring Installation -- Single-Ring Method

1. Place the single ring at the test location
2. Drive to approximately 5 cm depth using the same technique as above
3. For best accuracy, use the largest diameter ring available (90 cm or
   larger reduces lateral flow error) [@bouwer1986]. Single-ring
   measurements tend to overestimate true vertical infiltration because
   lateral divergence below the ring cannot be eliminated; the
   magnitude of overestimation decreases as ring diameter increases
   [@gregory2006].

### Initial Filling

1. Place a sheet of plastic or burlap on the soil surface inside the
   inner ring (and inside the annular space for the double-ring method)
   to cushion the water and prevent soil disturbance during filling
2. Gently pour water into the outer ring (annular space) first, then
   into the inner ring, to approximately 10--15 cm depth
3. Carefully remove the plastic or burlap
4. For the double-ring method, maintain the water level in the outer
   ring at approximately the same height as the inner ring throughout
   the test. This eliminates the lateral pressure gradient and forces
   flow beneath the inner ring to be vertical.

### Measuring Infiltration Rate

**Falling-head method (most common for EA Program):**

1. Record the initial water level in the inner ring and the start time
2. Allow the water to infiltrate. Record the water level at regular
   time intervals. Suggested intervals:

| Elapsed Time        | Recording Interval |
|:--------------------|:-------------------|
| 0--30 minutes       | Every 5 minutes    |
| 30--60 minutes      | Every 10 minutes   |
| 60--120 minutes     | Every 15 minutes   |
| 120+ minutes        | Every 30 minutes   |

3. When the water level drops to approximately 3 cm above the soil
   surface, refill to the original level and record the new starting
   level and time. Record each refill event.
4. Maintain the water level in the outer ring by refilling as needed.
5. Continue the test until the infiltration rate reaches a steady state
   (three or more consecutive readings with less than 10% change). This
   is the steady-state or "final" infiltration rate.
6. For most soils, steady state is reached within 1--3 hours. Clayey
   soils may require 4--6 hours or longer.

**Constant-head method (Mariotte bottle):**

1. Set up the Mariotte bottle to maintain a constant water depth
   (typically 5--10 cm) in the inner ring
2. Record the volume of water consumed from the bottle at regular
   time intervals
3. Calculate the infiltration rate from the volume consumed, the ring
   area, and the time interval
4. Continue until steady state is reached

### Ending the Test

1. Record the final water level, time, and cumulative number of refills
2. Remove the rings by rocking gently and pulling upward
3. Backfill the holes and restore the site
4. Record any observations about the wetting front depth, root
   channels, or other features visible after ring removal


## Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### Calculations

**Infiltration rate** for each time interval (falling-head method):

$$
f = \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t}
$$

where $f$ = infiltration rate (cm/h), $\Delta h$ = drop in water level
(cm) during the interval, and $\Delta t$ = duration of the interval (h).
If the ring was refilled during the interval, add the refill depth to
$\Delta h$.

**Cumulative infiltration:**

$$
F = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i \times \Delta t_i
$$

where $F$ = cumulative infiltration (cm) and $n$ = number of intervals.

**Steady-state infiltration rate** ($f_c$) is the final, approximately
constant rate, typically reported as the mean of the last three or more
consistent readings.

### Expected Ranges

Steady-state infiltration rates vary widely with soil texture and
structure:

| Soil Type / Condition                | Expected $f_c$ (cm/h)  |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Coarse sand, well-structured         | 5 -- 25+               |
| Sandy loam                           | 2.5 -- 7.5             |
| Loam, well-structured               | 1.0 -- 5.0             |
| Silt loam                            | 0.5 -- 2.5             |
| Clay loam                            | 0.1 -- 1.0             |
| Compacted or crusted soil            | less than 0.5          |

Values outside the range of 0.01--50 cm/h should be investigated for
measurement error or unusual soil conditions.

Rates measured at EA Program sites in the Pomona/Claremont area should
be interpreted in the context of the local aridic moisture regime, where
antecedent moisture is often very low and hydrophobicity may develop
under prolonged dry conditions [@hillel1998]. Urban and peri-urban soils
may show infiltration rates well below their textural expectation due to
compaction from foot traffic and construction [@lai2010].

### QC Requirements

- Conduct a minimum of three replicate tests per plot or treatment to
  capture spatial variability
- Record antecedent soil moisture and recent precipitation for each
  test; these strongly affect initial rates
- Verify that the outer ring water level is maintained throughout the
  test (double-ring method)
- Inspect ring installation for gaps between the ring wall and the soil;
  if gaps are visible, the test is invalid
- Ring insertion depth and ponded water depth both influence measured
  infiltration rate; standardize these dimensions across replicates and
  sites to ensure comparability [@gregory2006].
- Plot the infiltration rate versus time curve for each test. A
  monotonically decreasing curve approaching a constant value is
  expected. Erratic increases may indicate macropore activation or ring
  leakage.


## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type              | Disposal Method                             |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Test water              | Allowed to infiltrate on site; no disposal needed |
| Used plastic sheeting   | Standard trash                              |
| Used gloves             | Standard trash                              |

## Training Record

Before conducting infiltration tests independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) training
3. Observe a trained operator perform a complete double-ring
   infiltration test from ring installation through steady state
4. Demonstrate proper ring driving technique without ring deformation
   or soil cracking
5. Conduct at least one complete test under supervision and produce an
   infiltration curve that reaches steady state
6. Be signed off by the field lead or PI

## Appendix B: Example Calculation and Plotting {.appendix}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

# Example data from a falling-head double-ring test
# Ring inner diameter = 30 cm
ring_diam_cm <- 30
ring_area_cm2 <- pi * (ring_diam_cm / 2)^2

infiltration <- tibble(
  elapsed_min = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180),
  water_level_cm = c(15.0, 13.8, 12.9, 12.1, 11.4, 10.2, 8.8, 7.6,
                     5.8, 4.2, 2.8, 1.5)
)

# Calculate interval infiltration rates
infiltration <- infiltration %>%
  mutate(
    delta_h_cm = -diff(c(NA, water_level_cm)),
    delta_t_h = c(NA, diff(elapsed_min)) / 60,
    rate_cm_h = delta_h_cm / delta_t_h,
    cumulative_cm = cumsum(replace_na(delta_h_cm, 0))
  )

# Steady-state rate (last 3 intervals)
f_c <- mean(tail(infiltration$rate_cm_h[!is.na(infiltration$rate_cm_h)], 3))
cat(sprintf("Steady-state infiltration rate: %.2f cm/h\n", f_c))

# Plot infiltration rate vs time
ggplot(infiltration %>% filter(!is.na(rate_cm_h)),
       aes(x = elapsed_min, y = rate_cm_h)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = f_c, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = max(infiltration$elapsed_min) * 0.7,
           y = f_c + 0.3,
           label = sprintf("f[c] == %.2f~cm/h", f_c),
           parse = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    x = "Elapsed time (min)",
    y = "Infiltration rate (cm/h)",
    title = "Double-Ring Infiltration Test"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::



## Appendix C: Troubleshooting {.appendix}

| Symptom                       | Probable Cause                  | Corrective Action              |
|:------------------------------|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Water leaks around the outside of the ring | Insufficient insertion depth; gap between ring wall and soil | Drive ring deeper; pack bentonite or moist soil around the outside base |
| Infiltration rate increases mid-test | Macropore activation; preferential flow path opened | Note in field notebook; this may be a real feature of the soil. If clearly an artifact (ring shifted), restart. |
| Very slow infiltration (less than 0.1 cm/h) | Dense clay; surface crust; compacted layer | Continue test for at least 4--6 hours to confirm steady state; consider ASTM D5093 sealed-ring method |
| Rate never stabilizes         | Heterogeneous soil; macropores draining and refilling | Extend test duration; collect additional replicates; report the range rather than a single value |
| Ring deformed during installation | Rocks or roots; excessive force | Replace with a new ring at a nearby location |
| Soil disturbed inside the ring | Overly aggressive filling; ring bounced during driving | Restart at a new location; always use plastic sheeting during initial fill |
| Single-ring rate much higher than expected | Lateral flow beneath the ring | Use a larger-diameter ring (90 cm+) or switch to the double-ring method |
